lesson.hook: On September 23, 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter as it fired its engine to enter orbit around Mars. The investigation found that a ground software file called “Small Forces” had reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds, while the document both teams worked from, the Software Interface Specification, required newton-seconds. Every firing’s effect was underestimated by a factor of 4.45, and the spacecraft’s path had drifted far lower than the navigators believed. The specification named the right unit. What failed was the check: nothing in the process compared the delivered file against the spec before it was trusted. Every time you ask an AI for something, you are writing an interface specification for a contractor who works in seconds and rarely asks questions. This chapter is about writing it so that both of you can tell when it has been met.
lesson.overview: This chapter is the foundation for the rest of the book, and it works the same way whether you are asking for code, a screen, a picture or a sound. Section 1.1 explains why vague requests come back competent but generic: models fill every unmade decision with a default, quietly pick one reading of ambiguous words, follow your wording literally, and stumble over prohibitions. Section 1.2 introduces the six-part spec (goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples, output format), the requirements standards behind it, and current vendor advice to describe outcomes rather than steps. Section 1.3 turns qualities like “readable” and “feels good” into checks and shows how examples teach format. Section 1.4 covers usable output (including what replaced the old prefill trick), checks an agent can run itself, and revisions that change only what you name. Every section ends with a Prompt kit you can paste into a real tool today, and along the way you write the first spec for Lamplighter.
objectives: Identify underspecified, ambiguous and negatively phrased parts of a request in any medium, and predict the defaults a model will choose for them.
Write a six-part spec (goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples, output format) for a code task, an interface, an image and a sound effect.
Translate qualities such as “readable,” “feels good” or “punchy” into checks you or a coding agent can run, including Given/When/Then scenarios.
Request output in a usable shape, such as complete files, structured output or an assumption list, without relying on retired tricks such as prefill.
Write a scoped revision request that names a failing criterion with evidence and protects everything else from regressions.

sections.title: Why vague prompts fail
reading: Ask a coding agent to “make a cozy platformer about a lamplighter” and you will get a game. It will probably be a single web page with a rectangle for a hero, arrow keys to move, a jump, some floating platforms and perhaps warm orange colors standing in for “cozy.” It will not be the game you pictured, because almost nothing you pictured was in the request. Your sentence left most decisions open: where the game runs, which keys do what, how big the level is, what winning means, what “cozy” looks and sounds like. That condition is called **underspecification**: the request fits many different outputs, and the words do not choose among them. A model does not leave those decisions blank. It fills each one with a **default**, roughly the most typical choice for requests like yours (Chapter 2 explains the machinery), and that is why underspecified prompts tend to come back competent and average (Figure 1.1).

The same thing happens in every medium. Ask an image model for “a lamplighter at night” and the open decisions include the framing, where the light comes from, the style, the setting and the shape of the frame, so you get whatever combination the model treats as typical. Ask a sound generator for “a lamp lighting sound” and it has to guess whether you mean a match, a gas jet or a magical chime, how long the sound lasts, and whether it should ring out as if in a large hall. Ask for “a settings screen” and the model chooses which controls appear, in what order, and what happens when you press Escape. None of these results is wrong. Each is the model’s choice in a place where you did not make one, and you meet that choice only after it has been built into the result.

Anthropic’s guide to prompting its Claude models puts the problem in human terms. It asks you to think of the model as “a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows,” and adds that the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result [1]. Its test for a prompt, which it calls the golden rule, is to show the prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it; if they would be confused, the model will be too [1]. The guide also says that current Claude models are trained for precise instruction following, and that cuts both ways. If you write “can you suggest some changes,” Claude will sometimes give suggestions rather than make the changes, even when changes were what you meant, and if you want work that goes beyond the basics, you have to ask for it explicitly [1].

Underspecification has a cousin, **ambiguity**, where the words are present but can be read more than one way. “Make the lamps lighter” could mean brighter, paler, smaller on screen or lower in weight in the physics code. “Fix the button” assumes the model knows which button and what is wrong with it. “Make the enemies faster” leaves open movement, attack rate or spawn rate, and in which levels. Models are poor at catching this. Alisa Liu and colleagues built AmbiEnt, a set of 1,645 linguist-annotated examples, about a third of them ambiguous, and asked models to spell out the possible readings; crowdworkers judged GPT-4’s disambiguations correct only 32% of the time, against 90% for the ones written for the dataset [2]. Handed an ambiguous instruction, a model usually picks one reading and carries on without telling you it chose.

A third trap is the instruction written as a prohibition. A negation still puts the unwanted idea into the request, and models that turn descriptions into pictures handle it especially badly. Runway’s guide for its Gen-4 video model says the model is built to follow descriptions of what should happen, not of what should be avoided, and that “negative phrasing is not supported and may produce unpredictable or even opposite results” [3]. Its fix for “no camera movement” is to describe a locked camera instead [3]. Language models cope with negation better, but Anthropic’s guide still advises telling Claude what to do instead of what not to do [1]. “An empty street at dawn” is a decision. “No people” names the thing you did not want and leaves the street itself undecided. A few image tools offer a separate field for true exclusions, which Chapter 7 covers tool by tool.

People new to prompting leave these gaps for understandable reasons. J. D. Zamfirescu-Pereira and colleagues watched people without AI training design prompts for a chatbot. Their participants tried ideas opportunistically rather than systematically, overgeneralized from a single success or failure, and carried over habits from giving instructions to other people [4]. With a human colleague, shared context fills the holes: they were in yesterday’s meeting, and they know your taste. A model knows only what is in the conversation in front of it, plus general patterns from its training. Your taste, your project and your earlier decisions exist for it only if they are written down where it can read them.

The cure is not a longer prompt but fewer unmade decisions. Before you send a request, list the questions a capable stranger would need answered, then answer each one or hand it over on purpose. Handing it over on purpose, **explicit delegation**, sounds like this: “Choose the platform layout yourself, keep every lamp reachable, and list the choices you made.” Delegating is often the right call, since the model may know conventions you do not. Silent delegation is the problem, because you discover the decision only after it has been built into the result. The Prompt kit at the end of this section turns the stranger’s questions into a prompt you can run before the real one.

keyTerms.def: A request that fits many different outputs because it leaves decisions unstated.
The choice a model makes for a decision the request left open, usually the most typical choice for similar requests.
Wording that can reasonably be read in more than one way, such as “lighter” meaning brighter, paler or smaller.
Anthropic’s check that a prompt a colleague with little context could not follow will also confuse the model.
Stating what should be present (“an empty street,” “a locked camera”) instead of what should be absent.
Handing a decision to the model on purpose, with limits, and asking it to report what it chose.

templates.title: Decision audit (run before the real request)
templates.text:
Before you start the task, read my request below the way a capable stranger would.

<request>
[PASTE YOUR DRAFT PROMPT]
</request>

1. List every decision the request leaves open: where the result runs or will be used, size or length, style, format, scope, and anything else you would have to guess.
2. List every word or phrase that could reasonably be read more than one way, with its possible readings.
3. For each item, say which default you would choose if I said nothing more.

Reply as one numbered list.
templates.note: Works in any chat assistant, for code, images, sound or text. The defaults it lists are a preview of what you would have got. Answer each item or delegate it explicitly, then fold the answers into your spec (Section 1.2).

templates.title: Explicit delegation line
templates.text: You choose [THE DECISION, e.g. the platform layout] yourself. Stay within these limits: [LIMITS, e.g. every lamp reachable with one jump, no platform narrower than 2 tiles]. After the result, list each choice you made for it, one line each.
templates.note: Add it to any spec for decisions you are happy to hand over. The last sentence turns a silent default into one you can see, keep or change.

templates.title: Negatives to positives
templates.text:
Rewrite every negative instruction in the prompt below (no, don’t, avoid, without, never) as a description of what should be there instead, keeping the meaning. Show each change as Before -> After, then give the full rewritten prompt.

<prompt>
[PASTE YOUR PROMPT]
</prompt>
templates.note: Run it in a chat assistant before you send a prompt to an image or video generator. Runway documents that negative phrasing can backfire on its Gen-4 models (as of October 2026). If a tool has a dedicated negative-prompt field, true exclusions go there instead (Chapter 7).

example.title: Worked example: auditing Lamplighter’s first request
steps: Before: “Make a cozy platformer about a lamplighter.” Read it as a stranger would, and write down every question you would need answered before starting.

The questions: Where does it run, and in which language? Who lays out the platforms? Which keys? How big is the level? How do you win or lose? What does “cozy” mean in color, sound and pace? Placeholder art or finished sprites? What should come back: files, an explanation, both?
Mark each question. “Cozy” is ambiguous (a word with several readings); the other seven are underspecified (nothing was said). Eight decisions, none made.

Decide or delegate each one: the browser, plain JavaScript, arrow keys and Space, one screen-sized level, five lamps to light before a 90-second timer runs out, colored rectangles for art. Delegate the platform layout explicitly. Set “cozy” aside on purpose for this build, and leave the reply format to the full spec in Section 1.2.

After: “Make a first playable build of a 2D platformer called Lamplighter that runs by opening index.html in Chrome. Plain JavaScript and HTML canvas, 960×540, no libraries. Arrow keys move, Space jumps, E lights a lamp the player is touching. One level with five lamps; light all five before a 90-second timer ends to win; if the timer ends, show ‘Night fell’ and restart with R. Colored rectangles for all art. You choose the platform layout; keep every lamp reachable and list the layout choices you made.”
example.takeaway: Every question a stranger would ask is a decision; answer it or delegate it out loud, so nothing gets decided silently.

misconception.myth: A smart enough model will figure out what I mean.
misconception.fact: Capability helps a model carry out a request, not recover the parts you left out. The model has your words and its general training, so every missing decision gets a typical default. Anthropic’s own guidance says its current models follow instructions precisely and that work beyond the basics has to be asked for, and in the AmbiEnt study even GPT-4 usually failed to spell out the readings of an ambiguous sentence correctly.

practice.q: A reader asks an AI to “make the title screen pop more.” What is the main problem with this request?
choices: It is too short for the model to process
“Pop” has several possible readings and no result is defined, so the model will choose its own
It does not begin with a role such as “You are a designer”
It needs to be written in capital letters for emphasis
practice.explanation: “Pop” is ambiguous (more contrast, motion, bigger type, brighter color?) and nothing says what a finished result looks like, so the model fills both gaps with defaults. Length is not the issue, a role would not resolve the ambiguity, and capitals add emphasis but no information.

practice.q: You ask an image generator for “a lamplighter at night, nice lighting.” Name three decisions this request leaves to defaults, then rewrite it so that it settles two of them and delegates one explicitly.
practice.answer: Open decisions include framing (close-up or full figure), the light source and its color, the art style or medium, the setting, and the aspect ratio. A rewrite: “A full-body view of an old lamplighter on a rooftop at dusk, lit only by the warm lamp he has just lit, with a cool blue sky behind him, in a soft painted style, 16:9. Choose his pose yourself and tell me which pose you chose.”
practice.explanation: A good answer names concrete open decisions (not just “details”), settles at least two with specific words, and hands one over with a request to report the choice. Image tools that cannot reply in text still show their choice in the picture, so you check the pose by looking. Chapter 7 gives the exact vocabulary for framing and light.

practice.q: You ask a video generator for “rooftops at dusk, no camera movement, no people.” Which rewrite follows this section’s advice?
choices: “Rooftops at dusk, NO camera movement, NO people!”
“Empty rooftops at dusk, seen from a locked-off camera that stays completely still.”
“Rooftops at dusk. Please try hard to avoid any camera movement and avoid people.”
“Rooftops at dusk. Do not move the camera. Do not show people. Never add people.”
practice.explanation: The second choice describes what should be on screen (empty rooftops, a still camera), which is what Runway’s Gen-4 guide asks for. Capitals, “avoid” and repeated prohibitions all still name the camera movement and the people, the very things you wanted gone, and add no description of what should be there instead.

sections.title: The anatomy of a spec
reading: A **spec**, short for specification, is a description of something to be built, written so that one person can build it and another can check it. Requirements engineers have worked for decades on what makes such descriptions succeed. Their international standard, ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, lists characteristics that each individual requirement should have, among them that it be necessary, unambiguous, complete, singular (one requirement per statement), feasible and **verifiable** [1]. Two of these do most of the work in prompts. Unambiguous means only one reasonable reading. Verifiable means there is a way to show the requirement has been met. Singular is the quiet third: one statement, one requirement, so each can pass or fail on its own and a reviewer can point at the one that failed [1]. A prompt is a spec for a very fast contractor who starts work the moment you press Enter, so the same standards apply.

The hook of this chapter shows what a spec can and cannot do. The Mars Climate Orbiter’s Software Interface Specification defined the format and units of a file passed from ground software to the navigation team, and it called for thruster impulse in newton-seconds. The ground software file named “Small Forces” reported pound-force seconds instead, so the navigation software underestimated the effect of thruster firings by a factor of 4.45 [2]. Among the contributing causes, the investigation board listed the lack of complete end-to-end verification of the navigation software and related models [2]. The spec was right. It failed because nothing checked the delivered file against it, which is why every spec in this book ends with criteria you can check.

This book uses six parts for every spec (Figure 1.2). The **goal** says what you want and why. The **context** says who it is for, where it will be used and what already exists. The **constraints** set the limits. The acceptance criteria say how you will know it is done. The examples show what good looks like. The output format says what shape the answer should take. Each part prevents a particular failure. Without a goal the model works hard on the wrong thing; without context it guesses the platform and audience; without constraints it picks tools and scope for you; without criteria neither of you can tell when to stop; without examples it guesses the style; without a format you get prose when you needed files. Sections 1.3 and 1.4 cover the last three.

Notice what the six parts leave out: the steps. A spec describes the result and the limits and leaves the route to the builder, unless the route itself matters. Vendor guidance has moved the same way. OpenAI’s guide for its GPT-5.5 model, as of October 2026, recommends describing the expected outcome, success criteria, allowed side effects, evidence rules and output shape, and avoiding step-by-step process guidance unless the exact path matters; it warns that older prompts which spelled out every step can now narrow what the model tries [3]. The same logic sets a spec’s length. It should be as long as the decisions you need to fix and no longer: two sentences for a quick image, a page for an hour of agent work. Adjectives such as “amazing,” “polished” or “AAA quality” add length without adding a decision, because nobody can check them.

The goal is the part people skip most often, because it feels obvious to them. Anthropic’s documentation recommends giving the reason behind an instruction, not just the instruction. Its example replaces “NEVER use ellipses” with an explanation that the response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine that cannot pronounce them, and it notes that the model can generalize from the explanation [4]. A goal with a reason works the same way: “a first playable build, to test whether jumping and lighting lamps is fun before I spend time on art” tells the model to put its effort into controls and none into graphics. Context covers the rest of what lives in your head: your skill level, your machine, your files, your audience. The same guide suggests placing long documents near the top of a prompt, above the instructions, and wrapping each kind of content in its own labeled XML tag so instructions, context and examples are not confused [4].

A **constraint** is a limit the output must respect. Hard constraints are requirements (“plain JavaScript, no libraries, exactly two files”); soft constraints are preferences the model may trade off (“prefer short functions”). Say which is which. A useful special case is the **non-goal**, a statement of what is out of scope: “no menus, sound or touch controls in this build.” A model that has not been told the scope may reasonably add a feature or tidy a file nobody asked about, and a non-goal draws the line before it is crossed. Where you can, phrase limits as what to do instead of what to avoid, as Section 1.1 showed. Keep the tone calm, too. Anthropic’s guide notes that some recent Claude models (it names Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6) are more responsive to the system prompt than earlier ones, so wording such as “CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...” can now make them overreact, and it recommends normal phrasing such as “Use this tool when...” [4].

The six parts are not only for code. Google’s guide to prompting its Imagen image models builds a prompt from a subject, its context and background, and a style, and says prompts need not be long or complex but that most good ones are descriptive and clear [5]. Those three slots are the goal and the core constraints of an image spec, and the rest of the skeleton still applies. For Lamplighter’s title art, the context is a 1920×1080 title screen with the logo across the top third; the constraints are a soft painted style, a four-color palette and a 16:9 frame set with the tool’s own control; the acceptance criteria are a lamplighter in the right third and a top third calm enough to carry the logo; the example is a reference image; the output format is four variations as 16:9 PNGs, resized or upscaled to 1920×1080 if the tool’s native size is smaller. Figure 1.2 lays the code spec and the image spec side by side, and the practice below does the same for a sound.

keyTerms.def: A description of something to be built, precise enough that one person can build it and another can check it.
The outcome you want and the reason you want it, which tells the model where to spend effort.
The facts the model cannot know on its own: audience, platform, skill level, existing files and decisions already made.
A limit the output must respect; hard constraints are requirements, soft constraints are preferences that may be traded off.
An explicit statement of what is out of scope for this request, such as “no sound in this build.”
Stated so that there is a practical way to show whether the requirement has been met.

templates.title: Universal spec skeleton
templates.text:
<goal>
[WHAT YOU WANT], so that [WHAT IT IS FOR / WHY IT MATTERS].
</goal>

<context>
For: [AUDIENCE OR PLAYER]
Used or run in: [PLATFORM, SCREEN SIZE, ENGINE, TOOL]
Already exists: [FILES, ASSETS, DECISIONS ALREADY MADE]
About me: [e.g. not a programmer; I will test it by playing it]
</context>

<constraints>
Must: [HARD LIMITS: technology, size, length, palette, number of files]
Prefer: [SOFT PREFERENCES THAT MAY BE TRADED OFF]
Out of scope for now: [NON-GOALS]
You decide: [DECISIONS YOU DELEGATE, WITH LIMITS]
</constraints>

<acceptance_criteria>
1. [A CHECK ANYONE WOULD SCORE THE SAME WAY, WITH A NUMBER OR STATE]
2. Given [SITUATION], when [ACTION], then [OBSERVABLE RESULT].
3. [AN EDGE CASE]
</acceptance_criteria>

<examples>
[ONE TO FIVE EXAMPLES OR A REFERENCE. Copy: WHAT TO COPY. Vary freely: WHAT IS INCIDENTAL.]
</examples>

<output_format>
[EXACT SHAPE: complete files, JSON, a table, image size, audio format]
Then list every decision you made that this spec did not settle.
</output_format>
templates.note: Works in chat assistants and coding agents. The tags follow Anthropic’s advice to give each kind of content its own label; plain headings work too. Delete a part that has nothing to say rather than filling it with adjectives, and run the colleague test from Section 1.1 before you send.

templates.title: Image brief
templates.text:
[SUBJECT: who or what, doing what], [CONTEXT: where and when], in [STYLE OR MEDIUM, e.g. soft painted illustration].
This image is for [WHERE IT WILL BE USED], so [WHAT MUST STAY CLEAR, e.g. keep the top third calm and empty for a logo].
Composition: [FRAMING AND PLACEMENT, e.g. full figure in the right third, eye level].
Light and color: [LIGHT SOURCE AND DIRECTION; PALETTE, e.g. warm lamp light against a cool blue dusk sky; hex codes if you have them].
Mood: [ONE OR TWO WORDS].
templates.note: Built on the subject, context and style structure from Google’s Imagen prompt guide (checked October 2026). Write it as sentences, describe what should be there rather than what should not, and set aspect ratio, size and number of variations with the tool’s own controls where it has them. Write your acceptance checks down before you look at the results. Chapter 7 supplies the vocabulary for each line.

templates.title: Sound-effect brief
templates.text:
[SOURCE AND ACTION, e.g. a match strikes, then a small gas lamp catches with a soft whoomp and a faint glass ring].
It plays when [GAME OR APP EVENT], about [HOW OFTEN, e.g. 30 times per level], over [WHAT ELSE IS PLAYING, e.g. quiet music].
Shape: [START, e.g. sharp and immediate], [BODY, e.g. a short warm swell], [ENDING, e.g. a brief ring that fades to silence].
Length: about [N] seconds.
Space: dry and close, as if recorded right next to the source.
One sound only, with silence around it.
templates.note: One action per sound. Length, number of variations and file format are often settings in the generator rather than prompt text, so check its controls. Your acceptance checks might be: loudest at the start, fully silent at the end, still pleasant on the twentieth hearing. Chapter 9 explains attack, tail, and why game sounds are usually delivered dry so the engine can add the room.

example.title: Worked example: Lamplighter spec v0.1, part by part
steps: Goal: “A first playable build of Lamplighter, to test whether climbing and lighting lamps is fun before any art or sound is made.”
Context: “I am not a programmer. I will run the game by opening index.html in Chrome on a laptop. Nothing exists yet; these are the project’s first files.”

Constraints: “Hard: plain JavaScript and HTML canvas, no libraries, no build step, two files (index.html and game.js), canvas 960×540. Soft: keep functions short and commented. Non-goals: no menus, sound, saving or touch controls.”
Acceptance criteria and example: the checks written in Section 1.3, plus a text sketch of the level, a few rows of characters in which # is roof, L is a lamp and P is the player’s start.
Output format: “Reply with both complete files, then a bulleted list of every choice you made that this spec did not settle.”
Notice what is absent: no step-by-step instructions for writing the code, no adjectives, no capitals. Every line is a decision or a check.
example.takeaway: Each part of the spec closes one door the model would otherwise open on its own.

misconception.myth: A longer, more forceful prompt is always a better prompt.
misconception.fact: Length helps only when it carries decisions. Adjectives like “polished” or “stunning” cannot be checked, step-by-step instructions can narrow what a current model tries, and capitals are no substitute for a reason: Anthropic notes that aggressive “CRITICAL: You MUST” wording can make recent models overreact. A short prompt that settles the six parts beats a long one that circles them.

practice.q: In a spec, which part is “No sound or menus in this build”?
choices: Goal
Context
Non-goal, a kind of constraint
Output format
practice.explanation: It marks what is out of scope, which is a non-goal. It does not say what you want or why (goal), describe your situation (context), or say what shape the answer should take (output format).

practice.q: You want an AI to write button labels for Lamplighter’s menu. Which request best follows Anthropic’s advice to give the reason behind an instruction?
choices: “SHORT LABELS ONLY!!!”
“Labels must fit buttons 120 px wide at 16 px type, about 12 characters, because the menu has to fit small laptop screens.”
“You are the world’s best UX writer.”
“Write labels. Do not write long labels. Do not write long labels.”
practice.explanation: The second choice states a checkable limit and the reason for it, so the model can generalize (for example, preferring short verbs). Capitals and repetition add emphasis without information, and a flattering role sets no limit at all.

practice.q: Rewrite “a sound for when a lamp lights” as a six-part spec for a sound-effect generator.
practice.answer: Goal: “The sound that plays when the player lights a lamp in Lamplighter, so each lamp feels like a small reward.” Context: “It plays about 30 times per level over quiet music, and the game adds its own room echo.” Constraints: “Under 1 second, dry, a single isolated sound effect on its own.” Acceptance criteria: “Loudest at the very start, fades to full silence, no click at the end, still pleasant on the twentieth hearing.” Example: “A match strike, then a soft gas whoomp, then a faint glass ring.” Output format: “WAV, mono, 48 kHz, three variations” (a delivery choice for this project, set in the generator’s export settings or by converting afterwards, since prompt text rarely controls the file format).
practice.explanation: A strong answer gives a goal with its purpose, context about how often and over what the sound plays, checkable constraints such as length and dryness, criteria you can confirm by listening, a described example, and a delivery format. Chapter 9 explains why dry, mono sounds suit a game engine.

sections.title: Acceptance criteria and examples
reading: An **acceptance criterion** is a condition the result must meet to count as done, written so that anyone who checks it gets the same answer. Software teams attach a short list of them to each piece of work, and they are the verifiable requirements of Section 1.2 in practical form. Anthropic’s guide to evaluating prompts makes the point with a contrast: “The model should classify sentiments well” is a bad criterion, while an F1 score of at least 0.85 on a held-out test set of 10,000 posts is a good one, because it is specific and measurable [1]. A game or an app rarely needs statistics, but it always needs the same move: replace a quality you can only feel with a check you can run. Some checks you run with your own eyes and ears; others a coding agent can run itself, as Section 1.4 shows.

Most vague words in prompts can be translated (Figure 1.3). “Fast” becomes “the level appears less than two seconds after the page opens on my laptop.” “Readable” becomes a number. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, the W3C’s accessibility standard, are written almost entirely as criteria of this kind; success criterion 1.4.3 requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 between normal text and its background, and 3:1 for large text [2]. “Make the HUD text readable” leaves the model guessing, while “HUD text meets the WCAG 2.2 contrast minimum of 4.5:1” can be checked with any contrast tool. When a quality resists numbers, list what you could observe. “Cozy” art becomes four named colors and a lamp as the brightest spot in the frame; a “punchy” sound becomes a sharp start, a quick fade and a length under one second.

For behavior, one format works especially well. Behaviour-driven development, the practice built into the Cucumber testing tool and its Gherkin language, writes each scenario in three clauses: Given a starting situation, When something happens, Then an expected outcome follows [3]. “Given the player is touching an unlit lamp, when they press E, then the lamp lights and the lamp counter goes up by one.” Each **Given/When/Then scenario** is one check, it reads as plain English, and a coding agent can turn it into an automated test (Chapter 4). Writing three or four of them also pushes you to think about **edge cases**, the unusual situations where bugs hide: pressing E in mid-air, at a lamp that is already lit, or at the instant the timer reaches zero. Interfaces have edge cases too: the empty inventory, the name too long for its box, the button pressed twice.

Criteria say what must be true; examples show what good looks like. Putting a few worked examples in the prompt is called **few-shot prompting** (with one example, one-shot). Anthropic calls examples “one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude’s output format, tone, and structure,” and recommends three to five that are relevant to the real task, diverse enough to cover edge cases, and wrapped in example tags so the model can tell them apart from the instructions [4]. Diversity matters because a model copies more than you intend. If all three level sketches you provide are wide and flat, expect a wide, flat fourth. For pictures and sounds the example is usually a **reference**: an image, a clip or a recording that shows the look or sound you mean, which many generators accept directly (Chapters 7 to 9 cover how each tool uses one).

Research on why examples work supports that caution. Sewon Min and colleagues tested demonstrations on classification and multiple-choice tasks across 12 models and found that replacing the correct answers in the examples with random ones lowered performance only slightly; what the examples mainly conveyed was the set of possible answers, the kind of input text and the overall format [5]. For a vibe coder the lesson is practical. Examples are strongest at teaching shape: format, length, tone and structure. They also teach their accidents along with their intent, so vary everything you do not want copied, and if you include a **counterexample** of what you do not want, label it plainly as one.

Criteria and examples work best together. A criterion such as “each lamp description is one sentence of 15 to 25 words” can be checked but says nothing about voice; an example sets the voice but cannot say which of its features are required. Give both, and say which features of the examples are requirements and which are incidental. For Lamplighter, each lamp shows a one-line note when it is lit. The spec gives the criterion (one sentence, 15 to 25 words, present tense, no exclamation marks), three example notes in different moods, and a line saying that the examples set the voice while their subjects (a baker, a cat, a train) are free to change. The Prompt kit below packages both halves.

keyTerms.def: A condition the result must meet to count as done, stated so that anyone checking it gets the same pass or fail.
A behavior check written as a starting situation, an action and an expected outcome, from behaviour-driven development.
An unusual or boundary situation, such as an input at the exact moment a timer ends, where failures tend to hide.
Including a small number of worked examples in a prompt to show the model the format, tone and structure you want.
An image, clip or recording supplied as the example of a look or sound, instead of describing it only in words.
An example of what you do not want, clearly labeled so the model does not copy it.

templates.title: Acceptance-criteria checklist
templates.text:
Acceptance criteria for [FEATURE OR ASSET]. Each one passes or fails:

1. [MEASURABLE CHECK WITH A NUMBER AND UNIT, e.g. all HUD text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against what is behind it]
2. [OBSERVABLE BEHAVIOR, e.g. Esc opens the pause menu and Esc closes it]
3. Given [STARTING SITUATION], when [ACTION], then [RESULT].
4. Edge case: given [UNUSUAL SITUATION], when [ACTION], then [RESULT].
5. Everything that worked before still works: [EXISTING CHECKS OR TESTS TO RERUN].

How each will be checked: [METHOD, e.g. contrast checker, playing level 1, the test suite, a screenshot, listening on laptop speakers].
templates.note: Paste it into the acceptance-criteria part of any spec, or send it after a build as the checklist to verify against. If you cannot say how a line will be checked, it is still a wish: rewrite it with a number, a state or a behavior you could observe.

templates.title: Examples with required and incidental features
templates.text:
<examples>
<example>[EXAMPLE 1]</example>
<example>[EXAMPLE 2, DIFFERENT IN LENGTH, MOOD OR SUBJECT]</example>
<example>[EXAMPLE 3, AN EDGE CASE]</example>
</examples>

Copy from the examples: [WHAT IS REQUIRED, e.g. the voice, the sentence length, the structure].
Vary freely: [WHAT IS INCIDENTAL, e.g. the subject and setting of each one].
Every result must also meet: [CRITERIA, e.g. one sentence of 15 to 25 words, present tense].
templates.note: Anthropic recommends three to five relevant, diverse examples wrapped in tags (as of October 2026). Examples teach their accidents too, so vary everything you do not want copied and name what is required.

example.title: Worked example: from “the jump should feel good” to checks
steps: Before: “Make the jump feel good.” Ask what you would actually see or measure in a jump you like. Play a platformer you enjoy and watch the jump closely.

Turn what you see into numbers you can tune: “A full jump rises about 3 tiles (96 px with 32 px tiles). Tapping Space gives a shorter jump than holding it. The player reaches the top of a full jump in roughly 0.4 s.” These are your design targets, not universal truths, and Chapter 10 shows how designers tune them.

Add scenarios for edge cases: “Given the player walked off a roof edge less than 0.1 s ago, when they press Space, then they still jump.” “Given the player is in mid-air, when they press Space, then nothing happens.”
Add one example in words: describe the jump of a game you like in your own terms (quick rise, short hang at the top, faster fall) instead of only naming the game.
After: the request now has three numeric targets, two scenarios and one described reference. Each one can pass or fail the first time you play the build.
example.takeaway: “Feels good” becomes buildable when you write down what you would observe if it did.

misconception.myth: Acceptance criteria are paperwork for big companies, not something you need for a quick AI prompt.
misconception.fact: They matter more with AI, not less. A model produces a finished-looking result in seconds and will not tell you which of your unstated hopes it missed. Three or four checks take a minute to write and turn review from a vague impression into a list you can tick off, and a coding agent can run many of them itself.

practice.q: Which of these is an acceptance criterion?
choices: The pause menu should look professional
Pressing Esc during play opens the pause menu, and pressing Esc again closes it
Use your best judgment on the pause menu
The pause menu should be intuitive
practice.explanation: Only the second can be checked with a clear pass or fail. “Professional” and “intuitive” are qualities without a test, and “use your best judgment” is delegation, not a criterion.

practice.q: Write two Given/When/Then scenarios for this Lamplighter feature: the player falls off the bottom of the screen.
practice.answer: “Given the player is falling below the bottom edge of the canvas, when their box is fully off screen, then they reappear at the last lamp they lit (or at the start if none) and the timer keeps running.” “Given the player falls off screen at the moment the timer reaches zero, when the frame updates, then the ‘Night fell’ message shows and the player does not respawn.”
practice.explanation: Good scenarios name a precise starting state, a single triggering event and an observable outcome. The second scenario targets an edge case where two rules (respawn and time-out) could conflict.

practice.q: You give an AI three example lamp descriptions. All are exactly two sentences long and all mention brass. You ask for ten more. What is the likely result?
choices: The model will ignore the length and the brass, since only instructions count
The model will tend to copy the two-sentence length and the brass detail, so vary them unless they are requirements
The model will refuse because the examples are too similar
The examples will only work if each is labeled correct or incorrect
practice.explanation: Examples teach shape and surface features, as Min and colleagues found for format. Features shared by every example are likely to be copied. Vary what is incidental, or state which features are required.

sections.title: Output format and the first revision
reading: The **output format** is the shape of what comes back: which files, in which language, with what structure, at what length, in what markup. It is the most practical part of a spec, because it decides how much work you do after the model finishes. Ask for the form you will use. If you will paste code into files, ask for complete files with their names, not fragments. If you will compare options, ask for a table with the columns you need. Anthropic’s guide advises being specific about the desired format, telling the model what to do rather than what not to do (“Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs” instead of “Do not use markdown”), and matching the style of your prompt to the style you want back, since the formatting of a prompt can influence the formatting of the response [1].

When the output will be read by a program, ask for **structured output**: data in a fixed, machine-readable shape, usually JSON. For a Lamplighter level that might be an object with a width and height in tiles, a list of roofs and a list of lamps. In a chat window, show the exact shape with a short template. Through an API, Anthropic’s structured outputs feature, as of October 2026, constrains Claude’s responses to a **JSON schema** you supply, so that the result can be parsed reliably (the documentation notes exceptions, such as refusals and replies cut off at the token limit) [2]. Older tutorials taught a different trick, **prefill**: writing the first characters of the reply yourself, such as an opening brace. Anthropic’s guide says that starting with Claude 4.6 models, prefilled responses on the last assistant turn are no longer supported and return an error, and it points to structured outputs instead, or to a plain instruction such as “Respond directly without preamble” [1].

Two format requests pay for themselves on any larger task. The first is an **assumption list**: “after the files, list every decision you made that this spec did not settle.” It turns the hidden defaults of Section 1.1 into a list you can read in a minute, and it shows you what to add to the spec next time. The second reverses the order of work: **clarifying questions** before anything is built. Anthropic’s Claude Code guide suggests that for larger features you have the agent interview you about implementation, interface, edge cases and tradeoffs, write the result to a SPEC.md file, and then start a fresh session to build from it [3]. Questions cost a few messages and catch ambiguity before it is built in. Skip them for cheap drafts, where looking at a result is faster than answering questions.

No spec is perfect, so the first result starts a loop: build, check every acceptance criterion, revise (Figure 1.4). A good **revision request** names the failing criterion and the evidence, states the change, and fences off everything else: “Criterion 3 fails: a full jump rises about 6 tiles, not 3. Lower the jump to 3 tiles. Change only the jump constants in game.js and leave everything else as it is.” The fence matters. A model asked to fix one thing may change more than you wanted, and a change that breaks something that used to work is called a **regression** (Chapter 4). After each revision, recheck all the criteria, not only the one you fixed.

The strongest criterion is one the builder can check for itself. Anthropic’s Claude Code guide opens its best practices with this advice: “Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare” [3]. Its reasoning is that an agent stops when the work looks done, and without a check, looking done is the only signal available, so you become the one who catches every mistake [3]. The same guide asks for evidence rather than assertions: the test output, the command that was run and what it returned, or a screenshot of the result [3]. For images, sounds and game feel you are usually the check, so write your criteria down before you look or listen. Criteria chosen after seeing a result make it too easy to accept whatever came back.

Change one thing per revision when you can, and do not draw conclusions from one run. Melanie Sclar and colleagues changed only the formatting of prompts (separators, spacing, capitalization) while keeping the meaning the same, and on one open model, LLaMA-2-13B, accuracy on few-shot tasks varied by up to 76 percentage points across formats [4]. Their tasks were benchmarks, not creative briefs, but a prompt that worked last week can wobble on a small edit. The study of non-expert prompt designers found that newcomers often overgeneralized from a single success or failure [5]. If a result is good, write down what produced it; if it is bad, find the criterion it fails before you rewrite the prompt. A bare “that’s wrong, try again” gives the model no new information, so you are simply asking for another draw from the same request.

When you change your mind, change the spec too. Midway through a session it is tempting to steer only in chat (“actually make it four lamps”), but after a dozen such messages the real requirements are scattered across the conversation, and neither you nor the model can see them in one place. Keep the written spec as the single record of what you want and paste the current version when you start a new session. The Claude Code guide adds a rule of thumb for sessions that go wrong: if you have corrected the agent more than twice on the same issue, clear the conversation and start again with a more specific prompt that includes what you learned, because “A clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections” [3]. Chapter 5 explains why long sessions degrade, and Chapter 12 builds a whole project on the written spec.

keyTerms.def: Output in a fixed, machine-readable shape, usually JSON, so a program can use it directly.
A description of the fields a JSON object must contain and the type of each, used to define or enforce structured output.
Writing the opening of the model’s reply yourself so it continues from there; rejected on Claude models from the 4.6 generation onward (as of October 2026).
A requested list of every decision the model made that the spec did not settle.
A follow-up that names the failing criterion with evidence, the change to make, and what must stay the same.
A change that breaks something that previously worked.

templates.title: Bug report for a coding agent
templates.text:
Bug: [ONE-LINE SUMMARY, e.g. the player falls through the top-right roof]

Steps to reproduce:
1. [START, e.g. open index.html in Chrome and start level 1]
2. [ACTION]
3. [ACTION]

Expected: [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN; name the acceptance criterion it breaks]
Actual: [WHAT HAPPENS, with evidence: error text, console output, a screenshot, a measurement]
Worked before: [yes, in VERSION OR COMMIT / no / unknown]

How to fix it:
1. First write a test or check that fails because of this bug, and show me it failing.
2. Fix the cause, not the symptom. Change only [FILES OR AREA].
3. Run [TESTS OR CHECKS] and show me the output. Every existing acceptance criterion must still pass.
4. List every change you made and why.
templates.note: Expected versus actual, with evidence, is the heart of any bug report. The failing check first and the request for output follow Anthropic’s Claude Code best practices (October 2026). Chapter 4 adds stack traces, logs and version-control terms.

templates.title: Interview me first
templates.text:
I want to build [BRIEF DESCRIPTION]. Before writing anything, interview me about it. Ask about how it should work, what it should look and sound like, edge cases, and tradeoffs I may not have considered. Skip obvious questions, dig into the hard parts, and ask a few at a time.

When we have covered everything, write a complete spec with these parts: goal, context, constraints (including non-goals), acceptance criteria, examples and output format. Save it as SPEC.md, or show it to me if you cannot save files.
templates.note: Adapted from the interview prompt in Anthropic’s Claude Code best practices (checked October 2026). Use it for larger features. When the spec is done, start a fresh session to build from it, so the build begins with a clean context and a written spec.

templates.title: Scoped revision request
templates.text:
[N] acceptance criteria fail:
1. [CRITERION]: expected [TARGET], got [WHAT HAPPENED, WITH EVIDENCE].
2. [CRITERION]: expected [TARGET], got [WHAT HAPPENED, WITH EVIDENCE].

Make only the changes these fixes need, in [FILES OR AREA]. Keep everything else exactly as it is, including [WHAT MUST STAY THE SAME].
[OPTIONAL SCOPE FIX, e.g. Remove the music button; sound is out of scope for this build.]

Then recheck every acceptance criterion, not only these, show me the evidence for each, and list every change you made.
templates.note: Send it after any result that fails a check. If you have already corrected the same issue twice in one conversation, put what you learned into the spec and start a new session instead.

example.title: Worked example: the first revision of Lamplighter v0.1
steps: Run the build and check every criterion. Lamps light when touched and E is pressed (pass). The timer and both end messages work (pass). A full jump rises about 6 tiles instead of 3 (fail). A lamp lights while the player stands about 64 px away (fail). The model also added a music on/off button, which the spec never asked for.
Before, the tempting revision: “The jump is wrong and some other stuff is off, fix it.” It names no criterion, gives no evidence and puts no fence around the rest of the code.
Name each failure with its evidence and target: jump height about 6 tiles, target 3 tiles (96 px); lamp lights at about 64 px, target only when the player’s box overlaps the lamp’s box.
Fence off the rest and deal with the extra: sound is a non-goal for v0.1, so the button goes.

After: “Two acceptance criteria fail. (1) A full jump rises about 6 tiles; it should rise 3 tiles (96 px). (2) Lamps light from about 64 px away; they should light only when the player’s box overlaps the lamp’s box. Also remove the music button, since sound is out of scope for v0.1. Change only what these fixes need, recheck every criterion, and list every line you changed.”
Rerun and recheck all criteria yourself, not only the two that failed, to catch any regression, and add “no extra features beyond the spec” to the spec’s constraints for next time.
example.takeaway: A revision request is a small spec: the failing check, the change, and a fence around everything else.

misconception.myth: If the answer is wrong, keep regenerating, or keep correcting it in the same chat, until it comes out right.
misconception.fact: Regenerating samples the same request again, so you may get a result that is wrong in a new way, and you learn nothing about why. Find the criterion that failed and say so. If corrections keep failing, Anthropic’s Claude Code guide advises starting a clean session with a better prompt after two failed attempts, rather than piling more corrections into the same conversation.

practice.q: Your game code will load Lamplighter’s level data from the AI’s answer. Which output format request fits best?
choices: “Describe the level in a few paragraphs.”
“Return only a JSON object with width and height in tiles, a roofs list (x, y, w, h) and a lamps list (x, y), and no other text.”
“Make a nice level and show it to me.”
“Write the level as a table in your favorite format.”
practice.explanation: A program needs a fixed, machine-readable shape. The second choice names the fields, the units and the absence of extra text; through an API you could also enforce it with a JSON schema. Prose descriptions and free-choice formats would have to be converted by hand.

practice.q: A coding agent fixed the jump, but now the player falls through one of the roofs, which worked before. Name what has happened and write the revision request.
practice.answer: It is a regression: the fix broke behavior that previously worked. Revision: “The jump fix caused a regression: the player now falls through the roof at the top right (about x 22, y 6 in tiles), which was solid in the previous build. Restore solid collision on every roof while keeping the new 3-tile jump. Change only collision or jump code, list the lines you changed, and show me that the five original criteria still pass.”
practice.explanation: A good answer uses the word regression, gives evidence (which roof, that it used to work), keeps the earlier fix, fences the change and asks for evidence that all criteria still pass.

practice.q: When are clarifying questions from the model most worth the extra messages?
choices: For a quick image draft you can regenerate in seconds
Before an agent starts a multi-file feature whose requirements contain several ambiguous points
When you have already given a complete spec with acceptance criteria and examples
Never, because questions always slow the work down
practice.explanation: Questions pay off when a wrong guess is expensive and ambiguity is present, which is why Anthropic suggests an interview before larger features. For cheap drafts, looking at a result is faster; with a complete spec there is little left to ask; and “never” ignores the cost of building on a wrong reading.

interactives.title: Vague or exact?
interactives.intro: Sort each request, from code, interface, image and sound work. Ask yourself: could two different people check the result and agree on whether it was done?
buckets: Vague: leaves the decision to the model

items.text: Make the menu pop.
items.why: “Pop” has no agreed meaning, so the model picks one reading silently.

items.text: The pause menu opens with Esc and closes with Esc or the Resume button.
items.why: Two observable behaviors, each of which passes or fails.

items.text: Give the game a cozy vibe.
items.why: “Cozy” needs observable features: named colors, a tempo, the pace of play.

items.text: Use only these four colors: #1B2A41, #F2A541, #F5E9D3, #5C4B51.
items.why: Anyone can check every pixel against four hex codes.

items.text: A lamplighter at night, epic, masterpiece, 8k.
items.why: A pile of adjectives. Framing, light, style and setting are all still the model’s choice.

items.text: A full-figure lamplighter in the right third of the frame, lit only by the lamp he holds.
items.why: Placement and light source are both things you can see and check.

items.text: A cool sound for lighting a lamp.
items.why: “Cool” is a feeling; source, length and shape of the sound are all undecided.

items.text: A match strike into a soft gas whoomp, under one second, with no echo.
items.why: Source, length and space are stated, and you can confirm each by listening.

items.text: Make the enemies harder.
items.why: Harder how: faster, tougher, more of them, in which levels?

items.text: Split game.js into player.js, level.js and main.js without changing gameplay; all five acceptance checks must still pass.
items.why: A defined structure plus a test that guards against regressions.

interactives.title: Which part of the spec is this?
interactives.intro: Each sentence comes from one of two Lamplighter specs: the first playable build or the title-screen illustration. Sort it into one of the six parts, and notice that both specs use the same skeleton.

items.text: A first playable build, to test whether lighting lamps is fun before any art is made.
items.why: What is wanted and why.

items.text: A title-screen illustration that sets the dusk mood before the player presses Start.
items.why: The image’s purpose, which tells the model where to spend effort.

items.text: I will run it by opening index.html in Chrome on a laptop.
items.why: A fact about your situation the model cannot know.

items.text: The image sits behind the game logo, which covers the top third of the screen.
items.why: Where and how the result will be used is context.

items.text: Plain JavaScript and HTML canvas, no libraries, exactly two files.
items.why: Hard limits on how it may be built.

items.text: No menus or sound in this build.
items.why: A non-goal, the scope-setting kind of constraint.

items.text: Given the player touches an unlit lamp, when they press E, then the lamp lights.
items.why: A Given/When/Then scenario is an acceptance criterion for behavior.

items.text: The lamplighter stands in the right third, and the top third stays calm enough to carry the logo.
items.why: Two conditions you can check by looking.

items.text: Here is a reference image whose warm lamp light against a cool sky I want.
items.why: It shows what good looks like rather than stating a rule.

items.text: Return the level as JSON with a roofs list and a lamps list.
items.why: Structured output is a format request.

interactives.title: Rescuing a real request: the timer display
interactives.intro: A reader sent a coding agent this request for Lamplighter: “add a timer to the screen and make it look nice.” The agent drew small white numbers in the middle of the top edge, which vanished against the pale dusk sky. Improve the request one step at a time; think before revealing each answer.

steps.q: What did the original request leave undecided?
steps.a: Position and size, the time format (seconds or minutes and seconds), font and color, contrast against the background, what happens as time runs low, and what “nice” means. The agent chose a default for every one, and the contrast default failed.

steps.q: Turn the most important gaps into acceptance criteria.
steps.a: “The timer sits in the top-right corner, 16 px from both edges. It shows remaining time as m:ss. Its text meets the WCAG 2.2 contrast minimum of 4.5:1 against what is behind it (a dark panel behind the text is fine). In the last 10 seconds the text turns red.” Each line can now pass or fail.

steps.q: What output format, fence and evidence should the request ask for?
steps.a: “Change only the HUD drawing code in game.js. Reply with each changed function in full and say where it goes, then list any choices this request did not settle. Show me a screenshot of the HUD at the start of the level and one in the last 10 seconds.” The fence keeps the agent away from gameplay code, the list surfaces its defaults, and the screenshots are evidence you can check against the criteria.

steps.q: The new build puts the timer on top of the lamp counter, which was also in the top-right. Write the revision.
steps.a: “The timer now overlaps the lamp counter in the top-right. Move the lamp counter to the top-left, 16 px from both edges, with the same panel style. No HUD element may overlap another. Change only HUD layout code and recheck the four timer criteria.” The new rule about overlap becomes a permanent criterion in the spec.

interactives.title: The revision loop, in order
interactives.intro: Put the steps of a disciplined build-and-revise cycle in order, starting before the AI produces anything.
steps: Write the acceptance criteria, and how each will be checked, before seeing any result
Run or open the result and check each criterion, collecting evidence
Write down which criteria fail, with evidence such as a measurement, a test output or a screenshot
Send a revision request naming the failure, the change and what must stay the same
Check the new result against every criterion, not only the ones you fixed
Update the written spec with anything you added or changed your mind about
interactives.explain: Criteria come first so that the result cannot quietly redefine success. Checking comes before revising, because a revision without a named failure is just a second draw. Rechecking every criterion catches regressions, and updating the spec last keeps one written record of what you want instead of scattered chat messages.

slides.title: Chapter 1: How to Ask Exactly
bullets: Why vague prompts fail
The anatomy of a spec
Acceptance criteria and examples
Output format and the first revision
slides.notes: This chapter gives you the habits every later chapter builds on, for code, interfaces, images and sound alike. Each craft chapter adds vocabulary, but you will always put it into the same six-part spec and check it the same way.

slides.title: A spec that nobody checked
bullets: Mars Climate Orbiter, lost September 23, 1999
Spec required newton-seconds; the file gave pound-force seconds
Effect of thruster firings underestimated by a factor of 4.45
The spec was right; no step checked the file against it
slides.notes: The lesson is not that the spec was bad. A correct spec still fails if no one verifies the delivered work against it, which is why criteria come with every request.

slides.title: Underspecification and defaults
bullets: A vague request fits many outputs
The model fills each gap with a typical default
Same in code, images, sound and screens
Fix: answer each open question or delegate it explicitly
slides.notes: Use the golden rule from Anthropic’s guide: if a colleague with little context could not follow your prompt, neither can the model. List the stranger’s questions before sending, or have the model list them with the decision-audit template.

slides.title: Ambiguity, literal reading and negation
bullets: Words with several readings: lighter, faster, fix it
AmbiEnt: GPT-4’s disambiguations correct 32% of the time vs 90%
“Can you suggest” gets suggestions, not changes
Runway Gen-4: negative phrasing may produce opposite results
slides.notes: Current models follow your words precisely, so say the action you want and describe what should be present. “An empty street” is a decision; “no people” only names the thing you did not want.

slides.title: The six-part spec
bullets: Goal (with the reason)
Context
Constraints and non-goals
Acceptance criteria
Examples
Output format
slides.notes: Each part prevents one failure. Requirements engineering’s standard asks that each requirement be unambiguous, singular and verifiable, and those three tests apply to every line of a prompt.

slides.title: Outcomes, not steps; reasons, not capitals
bullets: OpenAI (GPT-5.5): outcome, success criteria, side effects, evidence, output shape
Avoid step-by-step process unless the path matters
Give the reason: the model generalizes from it
“CRITICAL: You MUST” can make recent models overreact
slides.notes: Vendors now agree that a clear result and clear limits beat a scripted procedure. Anthropic’s text-to-speech example shows a reason doing more work than an order in capitals.

slides.title: The same skeleton for any medium
bullets: Image: subject, context and style (Google Imagen guide)
Plus placement, light, palette and frame size
Sound: source, shape, length, space, delivery
Interface: layout, states and contrast targets
slides.notes: The parts of a spec do not change between media; only the vocabulary inside them does. Chapters 6 to 9 supply that vocabulary craft by craft.

slides.title: Acceptance criteria and examples
bullets: Pass or fail, same answer for anyone
WCAG 2.2: 4.5:1 contrast for normal text
Given / When / Then for behavior, plus edge cases
Three to five diverse examples; they teach their accidents too
slides.notes: Criteria turn review from an impression into a checklist. Min and colleagues found that demonstrations mainly convey format and the space of answers, so vary whatever you do not want copied.

slides.title: Output format
bullets: Ask for the form you will use
Structured outputs and JSON schemas for programs
Prefill is retired on Claude 4.6 and later (as of October 2026)
Assumption lists and interviews expose hidden defaults
slides.notes: Format decides how much work remains after the model finishes. Old tutorials that start the assistant’s reply for it no longer work on current Claude models; use structured outputs or a direct instruction instead.

slides.title: The revision loop
bullets: Give the agent a check it can run, and ask for evidence
Revise with failure, evidence, change and fence
Recheck everything to catch regressions
Two failed corrections: new session, better spec
slides.notes: A bare “try again” adds no information. Change one thing at a time, draw no conclusions from a single run, and keep the written spec as the record.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Every gap is a decision: make it or delegate it
Six parts: goal, context, constraints, criteria, examples, format
Make “done” checkable, and check it with evidence
Revise narrowly and keep the spec current
slides.notes: Your challenge is to rewrite three real prompts with the Prompt kit and write Lamplighter’s first spec. Chapter 2 explains the machinery behind defaults, randomness and context, so you can see why these habits work.

choices: A prompt that is too long for the context window
A request that fits many different outputs because it leaves decisions unstated
A model that has too few parameters
A word with two meanings
quiz.explanation: Underspecification means decisions were never stated, so many outputs fit. A word with two meanings is ambiguity, a related but different problem.

quiz.q: You type to a coding agent: “Can you suggest some ways to make the jump less floaty?” It replies with a list of ideas and changes no code. What is the best explanation?
choices: The agent is broken and should be restarted
The agent needs a role such as “You are a senior developer”
Current models follow your wording precisely, and you asked for suggestions; say “Change the jump so that...” if you want the change made
The request needed to be written in capital letters
quiz.explanation: Anthropic’s guide gives exactly this case: “can you suggest some changes” sometimes produces suggestions rather than edits. An imperative request with a target states the action you want. A role or capitals would not change what was asked for.

quiz.q: Which pair of requirement characteristics from ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 does this chapter treat as doing most of the work in prompts?
choices: Unambiguous and verifiable
Feasible and necessary
Complete and conforming
Singular and appropriate
quiz.explanation: Unambiguous means one reasonable reading, and verifiable means you can show it was met. Together they turn a wish into something a model can build and you can check.

quiz.q: A reader’s prompt to a coding agent says: “Make the HUD. Plain JavaScript. Two files max.” The agent spends its effort on an animated title screen. Which part of the spec was most clearly missing?
choices: Output format
Constraints
Examples
Goal, with the reason for the work
quiz.explanation: The constraints are present. What is missing is what the work is for and why, which would have told the agent to spend its effort on the HUD rather than on extras.

quiz.q: Which acceptance criterion best replaces “make the text readable”?
choices: “Text should be easy on the eyes.”
“Use a beautiful font.”
“All HUD text meets the WCAG 2.2 contrast minimum of 4.5:1 against its background.”
“Make sure players can read it.”
quiz.explanation: Only the third choice can be checked with a tool and gives the same answer to anyone who checks it. The others restate the wish.

quiz.q: According to Min and colleagues, what do demonstrations in a prompt mainly convey?
choices: The exact correct answer for each future input
The format, the kind of input and the set of possible answers
Nothing; examples have no measurable effect
The model’s training data
quiz.explanation: Replacing correct answers in examples with random ones hurt performance only slightly, which suggests examples mainly teach shape: format, input distribution and the space of possible answers.

quiz.q: An old tutorial tells you to force JSON from Claude by writing “{” as the start of the assistant’s reply in an API request. What happens with current Claude models as of October 2026, and what should you use instead?
choices: It works as before, so keep using it
It works only if temperature is set to 0
The model quietly ignores the brace and replies in prose
The request is rejected with an error; use structured outputs with a JSON schema, or ask for the shape directly
quiz.explanation: Anthropic’s guide says prefilled final assistant turns are no longer supported starting with Claude 4.6 models and return an error. Its recommended replacement for format control is structured outputs, which constrain the reply to your schema (with documented exceptions such as refusals and truncation).

quiz.q: After you fix the jump, the player starts falling through one roof that used to be solid. What is this called, and what habit would have caught it?
choices: A regression; rechecking every criterion after each revision
A hallucination; asking the model to be more careful
Underspecification; adding more adjectives
A default; regenerating the answer
quiz.explanation: A change that breaks something that used to work is a regression. Rechecking every criterion after each revision, not only the one you fixed, is how you catch it, ideally with a check the agent can run itself.

challenge.title: Three real prompts, rewritten with the Prompt kit
challenge.prompt: Find three prompts you actually sent to an AI tool in the last month: one for code, one for an image or a sound, and one for an interface or a piece of writing. For each, run the decision-audit template, then rewrite the prompt with the universal spec skeleton (or the image or sound-effect brief). Write the acceptance criteria before you run anything, run both versions in the same tool, and compare the results against those criteria.
challenge.deliverable: For each of the three prompts: the original, the audit’s list of gaps, the rewritten spec, and four to six sentences comparing the two results criterion by criterion.
rubric: Gaps are named concretely and labeled as underspecified, ambiguous or negatively phrased
Each rewrite contains all six parts, with at least two checkable acceptance criteria written before the run
At least one decision is delegated explicitly, with limits and a request to report the choice
Comparisons refer to the criteria, not just to overall impressions

challenge.title: Lamplighter spec v0.1 and its first revision
challenge.prompt: Write the complete spec for the first playable build of Lamplighter, using this chapter’s six parts, at least four acceptance criteria (two of them Given/When/Then scenarios with edge cases) and a text sketch of the level. Give it to a coding agent or chat assistant, ask for an assumption list and evidence for each criterion, run the result, check every criterion yourself, and write one scoped revision request.
challenge.deliverable: The spec (no more than one page), a pass or fail table for every criterion with evidence, the assumption list the model returned, and your revision request.
rubric: The goal includes its reason, and the constraints include at least one non-goal
Every acceptance criterion is verifiable by someone else
The check table gives evidence (a measurement, test output or a description of what happened) for each result
The revision names the failure, the change and the fence, and asks for all criteria to be rechecked

(ICLR 2024), Min et al. (EMNLP 2022), WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 and the Cucumber Book, checked figure numbering against the app's renderer (figures are numbered in section order), tested each of the 11 Prompt kit templates against the chapter's own advice, and re-solved all 16 multiple-choice keys, both sort exercises (20 items) and the order exercise blind before comparing.

corrections.after: Most vague words in prompts can be translated (Figure 1.3).
corrections.why: The app numbers figures in section order (dr-professor.html figHTML increments figNo per section). The section 1.3 figure (ch1-fig-4.svg, feeling-to-check) renders as Figure 1.3, so the text points to the wrong figure.

corrections.before: build, check every acceptance criterion, revise (Figure 1.3).
corrections.after: build, check every acceptance criterion, revise (Figure 1.4).
corrections.why: The section 1.4 figure (ch1-fig-3.svg, the build-check-revise loop) is the fourth figure in section order and renders as Figure 1.4.

corrections.before: Anthropic’s guide notes that recent Claude models respond more strongly to instructions than earlier ones
corrections.after: Anthropic’s guide notes that some recent Claude models (it names Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6) are more responsive to the system prompt than earlier ones
corrections.why: The live page (checked October 12, 2026) says: “Claude Opus 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.6 are also more responsive to the system prompt than previous models... may now overtrigger.” It names those two models and the system prompt, not recent models and instructions in general. The quoted CRITICAL/MUST wording is verbatim.

corrections.before: Do not start the task yet. Read my request below the way a capable stranger would.
corrections.after: Before you start the task, read my request below the way a capable stranger would.
corrections.why: The chapter's own advice (1.1 reading, Anthropic: tell the model what to do instead of what not to do) asks for positive phrasing; the template opens with a prohibition. The rewrite keeps the meaning.

corrections.before: Space: dry and close, with no echo or room sound.
corrections.after: Space: dry and close, as if recorded right next to the source.
corrections.why: This line is pasted into a sound generator, the kind of model the chapter warns handles negation badly (1.1 reading on Runway; the template kit's own Negatives to positives tool). Naming “echo” and “room sound” can pull them in. The positive description says the same thing.

corrections.before: Under 1 second, dry, one sound only; no music or voice.
corrections.after: Under 1 second, dry, a single isolated sound effect on its own.
corrections.why: The model answer is a prompt for a sound-effect generator but uses a prohibition (“no music or voice”), which contradicts the chapter's positive-phrasing advice for generative media models.

corrections.before: Output format: “WAV, mono, 48 kHz, three variations.”
corrections.after: Output format: “WAV, mono, 48 kHz, three variations” (a delivery choice for this project, set in the generator’s export settings or by converting afterwards, since prompt text rarely controls the file format).
corrections.why: WAV, mono and 48 kHz are reasonable project choices, not universal requirements. Most sound generators set format, sample rate and variation count through controls or plans rather than prompt text (the chapter's own Sound-effect brief note says so). Without that framing the answer suggests typing the format into the prompt will produce it.

corrections.before: Where does it run? In which language?
corrections.after: Where does it run, and in which language? Who lays out the platforms?
corrections.why: Step 3 promises to decide or delegate “each one” but then delegates the platform layout, which is not on the list. Figure 1.1 shows eight decisions that include Platform layout and not language. The merged question keeps the count at eight (step 2) and makes the list match both step 3 and Figure 1.1.

corrections.before: the output format is a PNG at 1920×1080 in four variations
corrections.after: the output format is four variations as 16:9 PNGs, resized or upscaled to 1920×1080 if the tool’s native size is smaller
corrections.why: Few image generators output exactly 1920×1080. Their native 16:9 sizes are usually smaller or different, for example Imagen's 1408×768 and Midjourney's 1456×816 at default settings. As written, the spec asks the tool for a size it usually cannot produce directly. The template note already says size is set through the tool's controls.

The row is for soft painted title art. A generated painted image always contains blends and anti-aliased edges, so a check that only four colors appear fails for every result. A tolerant check that the dominant colors match the palette is one that can actually pass or fail.

review.summary: Every Anthropic quotation (the brilliant-new-employee framing, golden rule, can-you-suggest example, ellipses example, CRITICAL/MUST, examples wording, prefill 400 on Claude 4.6+, Claude Code verification, interview and clean-session lines) matches the live pages. The OpenAI GPT-5.5, Runway Gen-4 and Imagen claims match vendor-page excerpts, and all 37 keys agree. The fixes are two swapped figure cross-references (1.3 and 1.4), one over-generalized Anthropic attribution, and seven alignment fixes so the templates, model answers, worked-example list and image checks follow the chapter's own positive-phrasing and tool-control advice.
